card.hook: Stand at the bottom of the Lotus Tower and you'll feel your neck bend back before you've even lifted your phone. It's 351.5 metres of one tall, simple shape, which makes it a very forgiving thing to photograph.
card.stand_here: Head for the base of the Lotus Tower on the Beira Lake waterfront in Colombo 01. The phone icon sits at the middle of the tower, within or beside its base area, so you'll be right at the bottom, looking up. For the full shape, walk back a little along the waterfront until the whole tower fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x right by the base, because it's the only way to fit much of the height in. Switch to 1x once you've stepped back for tidier, less stretched shots. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it from a distance to pick out the top.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is lovely. The light softens, and the tower's colour-changing lights show up against the darkening sky. After dark, switch on night mode and tuck your elbows into your body to keep the lights sharp.
card.selfie_here: Head inside to the Pixel Bloom digital art zone, where you can pose in front of the moving lights and effects. Use the front camera and hold it a bit away from you so the glow fills the background (the tower itself won't be behind you here).
card.ask_someone: In the park and garden at the base, on McCallum Road, ask the person to step back along the wide paths until the whole lotus-shaped tower fits in the frame, with you standing in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed inside the tower, and it's generally fine on the observation deck, but respect any restrictions in the dining areas. The waterfront area is open to walk around, but check current access details before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with the lake in front, then one close-up of the textured base, and see if friends can tell they're the same tower.
card.good_to_know: The tower is shaped like a lotus flower, which stands for purity in Sri Lankan culture, and the base echoes a lotus throne. Work started in January 2012 and the opening ceremony was on 16 September 2019. As of 2019 it was the tallest self-supported structure in South Asia, and it carries broadcasting antennas as well as an observation gallery.

card.stand_here: Stand across the street from the Khan Clock Tower at the Pettah Market entrance, and face the tower. Your goal is the tower on top and the crowd at its base below.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the whole tower and the crowd fit in. If traffic or people stop you stepping back, switch to zoom 0.5x. Save zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for the clock face and stall details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the tower on one vertical line, then tap the people at its base and slide darker a touch so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Weekdays or Saturday mornings give you the busiest, liveliest scenes. One guide says Sunday retail is reduced and wholesale is closed, so the market is much quieter then.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the four-storey clock tower at the market's main entrance, with the tower behind you. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a bit low so the whole tower fits over your shoulder.

card.good_to_know: Pettah Market is also called Manning Market. The Khan Clock Tower was built by the family of Framjee Bhickajee Khan, a well-known Parsi family from Bombay with big business interests in Sri Lanka, who owned the Colombo Oil Mills. card.hook: Most hotels make you walk inside to feel the history. This one spreads its whole colonial front along the seafront, with a big lawn and the Indian Ocean right beside it, so one frame can hold the lot.
card.stand_here: Stand at the northern end of Galle Face Green, where the promenade begins beside the hotel. The hotel is directly south of that point, about 1 minute on foot, so face south with the hotel on one side of the frame and the lawn and sea beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the long front and the sea into one frame, then try 1x for a calmer, more natural view. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is good for details of the building.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the horizon up with one of the horizontal lines so the sea sits level.
card.best_time: Go in the late afternoon, roughly 4 to 5 pm, when the light is softer. You'll also find a spot before the crowds build.
card.selfie_here: Try the black-and-white Chequerboard, nearby the hotel and facing the sea for the sunset. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more sky, and check your screen to see what's behind you before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Galle Face Green lawn or promenade and shoot back toward the hotel, while you stand with the hotel frontage behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The hotel is private property, so take your photos from the public green rather than going into the hotel grounds. If you plan to visit the hotel's restaurants or museum, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Take one photo where the sea is dead level on the gridline, then one where you've left just enough sky above the roofline to give the building room to breathe.
card.good_to_know: The Galle Face Hotel was founded in 1864 by four British entrepreneurs and began as a Dutch villa called Galle Face House. It's named after Galle Face Green, the lawn it faces. The south wing, designed by Edward Skinner, was finished in 1894, and the north wing's refurbishment finished in 2015.

card.hook: Step inside Gangaramaya's main hall and everything fights for your attention: huge seated Buddhas, golden statues, decorated walls and ceilings. Pick one thing and make it your picture.
card.stand_here: Stand at Gangaramaya Temple itself, right where the phone icon sits, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Face from the entrance side of the main hall towards the Buddha statues.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x to fit the whole hall with the seated Buddhas and the decorated ceiling. Switch to 1x for a single statue or a detail on the walls, and try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for gold details that are further away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the walls and pillars straight, then tap the face of a statue and slide it a little darker so the gold doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, before the crowds build. Light comes through the window screens and throws patterns across the floor, which adds depth to your shot.
card.selfie_here: Head to the floating platforms and wooden walkways of the Seema Malaka pavilion, out over Beira Lake. It's described as the most photographed spot in the city, and the walkways give you a lakeside backdrop of the temple's architecture. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the pavilion over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the lakeside edge of the temple grounds and ask someone to step back and shoot so the temple and its reflection on the water are both in frame.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship, so cover your shoulders and knees, and expect to take your shoes off before the prayer halls. Never pose with your back to a Buddha statue, and keep the flash off. Cover any Buddha tattoo before taking photos. Some shrine rooms may restrict photography, so check the signs or ask a temple attendant.
card.challenge: Find the patterns the window screens throw across the floor and catch one in your frame with a Buddha in the background.
card.good_to_know: Gangaramaya began as a small hermitage on marshy land beside Beira Lake and was completed in the late 19th century. Its architecture mixes Sri Lankan, Thai, Indian and Chinese styles. The compound also has a stupa, a museum, a library and a Bo tree grown from a sapling brought from Anuradhapura.

card.hook: Kites bobbing overhead, a ship creeping along the horizon, and a snack vendor somewhere behind you: Galle Face Green at sunset is a bit of a party. It's one of the easiest places in Colombo to get a sunset photo.
card.stand_here: Stand at the southern tip of Galle Face Green, on the sea side, and face the open ocean. The main part of the green lies to the north-west, about 5 minutes on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the sunset and the horizon. Go to zoom 0.5x to fit in more sky and the kite flyers. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a passing ship.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the brightest part of the sky and slide it a little darker so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Get there about 15 minutes before sunset so you can settle in and try a few shots, then stay through the last hour of daylight. Weekend evenings are busier, so expect company.
card.selfie_here: At the southern tip, use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and tilt it up so the sea and sunset sky fill the space behind your shoulder. Or try the open lawn in the late afternoon, with kites in the sky behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone at the northern entrance, where the promenade begins beside the Galle Face Hotel, to take your photo with the hotel's colonial architecture behind you, and check the framing on your screen.
card.rules_and_safety: The shore is rocky, not sandy, and vendors and stray dogs gather on the lawn. Keep an eye on your phone and bag, and agree any tuk-tuk fare before you set off. It's an open public park, but check the official site for events or restrictions.
card.challenge: Catch one kite in the sky with the sun just beside it, and give yourself bonus points if a ship sneaks in on the horizon.
card.good_to_know: The green covers about 5 hectares and runs for roughly 500 metres along the coast. Its promenade was laid out in 1859 under Governor Sir Henry George Ward, and in the 1820s the green was used for horse racing. Building work for the Port City is gradually changing the skyline.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for people, food stalls and trains. Switch to zoom 0.5x to fit in the station roof and the length of a platform, or try zoom 2x for a closer shot of a train or stall if your phone has it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put a walker or a train on one of the lines, and use the patch of light on the floor as your foreground.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime, when the light comes through the roof. It's a major commuter hub, so expect crowds at busy times.
card.selfie_here: Head outside to the open ground in front of the station's long main front and put the grand facade behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone a little low so the building fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask before photographing anyone close up, keep out of the way of people with luggage, and follow staff instructions. Keep clear of the platform edge while you shoot, use the footbridges to move around, and check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait, don't chase: see if you can catch one commuter stepping into a patch of light, with a train waiting behind them.
card.good_to_know: Fort is the end of the line for most intercity trains in Sri Lanka. The present station opened in 1917 on land reclaimed from the Beira Lake. It was built along similar lines to Manchester Victoria station.

card.hook: Pettah is a busy jumble of plain buildings, and then there's the Red Mosque, dressed up like a giant red-and-white candy cane. You can't miss it, and honestly, you won't want to.
card.stand_here: Stand on 2nd Cross Street, on the opposite side from the mosque's front, so the whole striped facade is across from you. The mosque lies to the east of you, so face east with your phone upright and level.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the stripes, domes and minarets into one frame. If you can step back far enough, 1x gives a calmer, less stretched look. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the domes, clock tower and stripe patterns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them so the minarets don't lean, then tap the facade and slide it a little darker so the white stripes keep their detail and the red stays rich.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the light is said to suit the facade best. Skip prayer times, including Friday around noon.
card.selfie_here: Try the arched doorway on the facade, with the red-and-white front behind you, using the front camera. Another option is the front courtyard with the facade behind you. Neither has an exact map spot, so check them when you arrive and see what works.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pedestrian side of 2nd Cross Street, across from the mosque and opposite the textile shops, while you pose near the arched doorway so the full facade fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship, so dress modestly with arms and legs covered, keep photos respectful and be ready to move aside for people going in. The narrow streets can be crowded and busy with traffic, and one guide suggests ignoring anyone nearby offering paid city tours.
card.challenge: Fill the whole frame with stripes, keep both minarets perfectly straight against the gridlines, and see if you can do it without a single scooter sneaking in.
card.good_to_know: Jami Ul-Alfar, known locally as the Red Mosque, was built between 1908 and 1909 for the local Indian Muslim community. Its designer and builder, Habibu Lebbe Saibu Lebbe, worked from pictures and details of Indo-Saracenic buildings supplied by South Indian traders. In 1975 an expansion began that was meant to raise its capacity to 10,000 worshippers.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on 2nd Cross Street, on the opposite side from the mosque's front, so the whole striped facade is across from you. The mosque lies to the east of you, so face east with your phone upright and level.

card.hook: Ever tried to squeeze a whole museum into one photo and ended up with a leaning tower? This big, formal building has straight lines, steps, columns and arches, so it's a gift to a phone camera once you keep things level.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the Colombo National Museum itself, and face the front of the building. Think of it as your starting point, then wander a few minutes for other views where access allows.
card.zoom: Step back and use zoom 0.5x to fit the whole wide front in, with gridlines on so the roofline or the base of the walls sits along a horizontal line. For a tighter shot, switch to zoom 1x and frame one arch, doorway or row of windows, or try 2x-5x for details if your phone has them.
card.make_it_pop: If the front looks washed out, tap the brightest part of the sky or wall and drag the slider to make it a little darker; if the building is in shade against a bright sky, tap the wall so it gets brighter instead.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer, warmer light on the front than midday. Thin cloud works well too, because it avoids harsh shadows under the roof and arches.
card.selfie_here: Walk the path lined with banyan trees that leads to the museum, then use your front camera with the white colonial building behind you. The fountain area in front of the museum is another photo spot, and the fountain is lit up at night, but check on site which way the building sits behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand in front of the main entrance and frame the full facade with its grand pillars, while you stand with the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash isn't allowed inside the museum. Photography rules inside can differ from the grounds, so ask or check the official site before you go.

card.good_to_know: This is the largest museum in Sri Lanka, and it opened in 1877. Government architect James George Smither designed it in the Italian style and finished it in 1876. card.hook: Here's a lazy way to get a great photo: stand on the grass and let the lawn do the work. The big white Town Hall across the road sits behind it like a wedding cake on a green tablecloth.
card.stand_here: Head for the Town Hall in Cinnamon Gardens, then walk about 143 m (a short walk) to the south-west to reach Viharamahadevi Park. Stand on the lawns on the side facing the Town Hall and face the building across the road.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the Town Hall across the lawns. Try 0.5x if you want more grass and sky, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the building's details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the Town Hall on the centre line, let the lawn fill the lower third, and keep your phone level so the building's vertical lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is the time guides recommend for the Town Hall view. If you want a clean frame, wait for a gap in the people.
card.selfie_here: Head to the lotus pond beside the golden Buddha statue and stand at the pond edge, ideally at golden hour. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the Buddha statue in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the Town Hall side of the road, across from the park, and frame you with the golden Buddha statue and the park beyond.
card.rules_and_safety: The lake's suspension bridge has been called wobbly, so take care if you pose on it. Check the official site for opening times and event days, and ask event staff before photographing at Open Air Theatre events.
card.challenge: Get the whole Town Hall in the frame with a big green stripe of lawn underneath, and no stranger walking through it. Patience is the whole game.
card.good_to_know: Viharamahadevi Park is Colombo's oldest and largest park. The British built it as Victoria Park, and it was renamed after Queen Viharamahadevi on 18 July 1958. The Buddha statue replaced the original statue of Queen Victoria.

card.hook: Long, low wings, deep verandas and a whole row of arches that repeat like a drumbeat: this old Dutch building was made for photos where you just stand back and let the lines do the work.
card.stand_here: Stand on Hospital Street, right in front of the main façade, and face the building. The old hospital sits to the east of you, with the street in front and the Fort streetscape around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole frontage. If the street is too narrow for the full length, switch to zoom 0.5x and keep the building away from the edges so the lines don't look stretched. Use zoom 2x or higher for arches, roof details and verandas.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the roofline up with a horizontal grid line so the walls stand straight, and keep a little street at the bottom to show where you are.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows under the verandas. Midday sun makes the arches look harsh and contrasty.
card.selfie_here: Head into the central courtyard of the precinct and use the front camera with the tiled eaves and arched walkways behind you. Try zoom 0.5x if you want more of the arches in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Casual photos for personal use are generally fine, but professional or commercial shoots may need permission. Ask before photographing inside shops or during private events.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the arches and their shadows repeat the most, and fit as many of them as you can in one photo.
card.good_to_know: This is thought to be the oldest building in the Fort area, and it's believed to have been in use by 1681 caring for officers, staff and seafarers of the Dutch East India Company. It later became an apothecaries' base and a police station, was badly damaged in 1996, and reopened in 2011 as a shopping and dining precinct. It has five wings around two courtyards, and the walls are about 50 cm thick.

card.hook: Let's be honest: you're not here for the shopping, because most of the stalls are closed these days. You're here for red-roofed pavilions sitting on a lake in the middle of busy Colombo, and that's still a lovely scene.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon in the middle of the market, on the lakeside walkways. Face out so you can see the pavilions and the water together.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the pavilions, walkways and water into one shot. Then try 1x for a natural look, and 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out roof lines and reflections.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap the pavilions, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky and water keep their colour.
card.best_time: Go in the late afternoon towards sunset, when the light on the water is at its warmest. Check locally before you set off if you want to see any stalls open.
card.selfie_here: Try the west entrance, standing in front of the carved wooden sign that reads 'The Floating Market'. You can also try the bridge over Beira Lake with the red-roofed pavilions behind you, but check it's still there first. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the market fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine, but ask before taking close-up shots of vendors. The lake water can look murky and smell strong in hot weather, so keep your shots wide.
card.challenge: Line up a walkway rail so it points straight at a red roof, then catch that roof's reflection in the same shot.
card.good_to_know: The market opened on 25 August 2014 with 92 stalls, some of them on boats on Beira Lake. One aim was to give street traders a proper place to work, so they weren't crowding the footpaths in Pettah. It sits on Bastian Mawatha, between the Central Bus Stand and Colombo Fort railway station, and a redevelopment is under discussion.

card.hook: By day, Beira Lake is a bit of a green, algae-coloured shrug. Wait for the light to drop and the lit buildings start showing up in the water, and it turns into a different place.
card.stand_here: Stand at Colombo City Centre, where the middle of the lake is about 1.2 km to the south-east. Face that way and look out across the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full dusk view across the lake. Then try zoom 2x to pick out the reflections of the lit buildings. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want lots of sky, because it also pulls in clutter at your feet.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the lit buildings, then drag the slider to make the shot a touch darker so the lights don't burn out.
card.best_time: Come a little before sunset so you can try a few frames as the sky changes. The sweet spot is blue hour, when the sky still has colour and the city lights are on.
card.selfie_here: Try the wooden walkways and floating platforms of the Pettah Floating Market on Beira Lake. It sits on the water, so the lake ends up right behind you, and the boats and water look especially good in the evening. Use the front camera at arm's length, or try zoom 0.5x to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the lakeside promenade facing Seema Malaka Temple and step back until the whole temple and its bridge fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The exact area of Colombo City Centre that's open to the public for this view isn't confirmed, so check with the building before you go. At Seema Malaka, cover your shoulders and knees, and an entrance charge may apply. Don't pose with your back to a Buddha statue, and check before photographing inside. One guide says the lake area is safe to explore in daylight and early evening.
card.challenge: Catch a stork, pelican or monitor lizard at the water's edge, then get the lit skyline reflected behind it.
card.good_to_know: The Portuguese created Beira Lake as a moat to protect their fort, by joining a stream to a marshy ditch they had dug. It once covered about 1.65 km2 and is now about 0.65 km2. Storks, pelicans and monitor lizards live here. The smell is strongest in dry weather, so don't be surprised if you notice it near the water.

card.hook: A bronze statue stands guard in front of a pale stone pavilion, and the whole thing looks like a very grand stage set. Lucky for you, the statue makes the perfect foreground.
card.stand_here: Stand right in front of the hall, at the head of the monument, by the statue of D. S. Senanayake in Independence Square. Face the pavilion so the statue sits in front of the columns.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the statue with the pavilion behind it. Go 0.5x to fit the whole width of the hall and the lawns, then 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved stonework and columns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the statue on one third of the frame, then tap the statue and slide the brightness a little darker so the pale stone doesn't turn white against the sky.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the stonework and fewer people on the lawns. Skip national ceremony days if you want a clear view of the statue.
card.selfie_here: Try the front steps of the Independence Memorial Hall: use the front camera, go 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the hall rise behind your shoulder. For a close-up, stand beside the D. S. Senanayake statue instead. That one is more about the statue than the whole building.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the green lawns facing the front of the hall, so the whole building fits in the frame, while you pose on the steps.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography of the site is generally allowed, but be respectful of the place. Skip the flash around people, especially if a ceremony is nearby. Inside the museum, follow staff guidance. It's pretty exposed out there, so bring sun protection. Be wary of anyone on the lawn offering paid photos with animals.
card.challenge: Walk slowly around the statue and take three shots, so you can see the pavilion change behind it each time.
card.good_to_know: This is Sri Lanka's national monument to independence from British rule, marking 4 February 1948. It stands where the first parliament was opened that day, in Independence Square, once called Torrington Square. The design follows the Magul Maduwa, the royal audience hall of the Kingdom of Kandy, and was drawn up by eight architects led by Tom Neville Wynne-Jones.

card.hook: Picture a blue-roofed temple floating on a city lake, with wooden walkways wobbling gently out to it. That's Seema Malaka, and it's calmer than it has any right to be in the middle of Colombo.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon, which sits right at the temple on Beira Lake, a few hundred metres east of Gangaramaya Temple. Stand on the lake shore at the foot of the walkway and face out at the temple, with the water in front of it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the temple and the lake together. Tap 0.5x to squeeze in more platforms and water, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the Buddha statues and roof details from the shore.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the temple on one line and keep the water in front, then tap the temple and slide a little darker so the blue roof keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is best. The light is softer and the lake is usually calmer.
card.selfie_here: Walk partway out along the pontoon walkway from the shore, then turn around so the temple platforms fill the frame behind you. Use the front camera and try 0.5x to fit more in. Views back toward the Colombo skyline are among the most photographed here too.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to take your photo from the far bank of Beira Lake, opposite the temple on the side away from the main gate, so the whole temple sits in the lake behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Take your shoes off before the platforms and cover your shoulders and knees. Never pose with your back to a Buddha statue, and keep a respectful distance from anyone praying or meditating. Check at the gate whether there's an entry fee.
card.challenge: Find a seated Buddha statue on the platform edge and use it as your foreground. Can you spot which hand gesture it's showing, and get the timber pavilions and lake behind it?
card.good_to_know: Seema Malaka is a Buddhist temple used mainly for meditation and rest rather than worship. It was first built in the late 19th century, but the original slowly sank into the water in the 1970s. In 1976 the Sri Lankan architect Geoffrey Bawa redesigned and rebuilt it, and that's the temple you see today.

card.hook: Four stone lions sit at the foot of a bright white tower, and they're easily the best photo buddies in this corner of Colombo. Meet them before you start snapping the lighthouse.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon, right at Colombo Lighthouse on Galbokka Point, in the garden and plaza facing the ocean. Face the tower so the open sea and sky sit around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole tower with sky around it. If you're close and the top won't fit, switch to 0.5x and hold your phone level. Zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) is great for the lions or a ship in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands tall instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Sunset is the time most guides recommend. Get there a little early so you can try a few angles.
card.selfie_here: Sit or stand beside the four seated lion statues at the foot of the tower, with the lighthouse rising behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if you want the tower to fit above your shoulder. The landscaped garden around the base is a nice green backdrop too.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the plaza in front of the tower and step back from it, so they can fit its full height while you pose by the lions.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower can be viewed from outside but not climbed. It's next to Naval Headquarters and photography is restricted in some directions, so look for signs, follow staff or guards, and aim away from naval areas. Don't photograph Navy personnel directly, and keep a safe distance from restricted areas.
card.challenge: Get a lion's-eye shot: crouch low next to one of the stone lions with the whole white tower rising behind it.
card.good_to_know: The lighthouse was built in 1952 and stands 29 metres high on a concrete base about 12 metres tall. A naval gun battery sits at its base, and the Sri Lanka Navy has used it for traditional gun salutes. Don't mix it up with the Old Colombo Lighthouse and Clock Tower in Fort, which is a different building.

card.hook: The narrow stairs to the choir loft squeeze right past a bell that weighs 4,300 lbs, so say a polite hello on your way up. At the top, the whole cathedral opens out below you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, inside St. Lucia's Cathedral, up in the choir loft. Face down the nave toward the sanctuary and the Archbishop's throne.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the sanctuary and the throne. Go to 0.5x if you want more of the nave and ceiling, and try 2x (or higher, if your phone has it) for the throne, the statues or one stained-glass window.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the central aisle up with the middle of the frame so the walls stay straight, and keep the throne in the lower half so the arches fill the top.
card.best_time: Go on a weekday morning, when there are fewer people and daylight makes the stained glass glow. The road up to the cathedral is one-way and gets busy around school closing time, so aim to arrive earlier or later in the afternoon.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x and tilt it up a little so the building fits over your shoulder. Hold the phone slightly higher than your face so more of the background gets in.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep flash off and stay quiet during services. Sundays are very crowded. Scaffolding from restoration work may block the facade or the interior, so be ready to change your angle. Check the official site or the parish before you go for visiting arrangements and access to the choir loft.
card.challenge: Take one photo where the aisle is dead centre and both walls look perfectly straight, then go outside and see if you can fit the columns, all seven statues and the cross on the dome in a single frame.
card.good_to_know: St. Lucia's is the seat of the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Colombo and is considered the oldest and largest parish cathedral in Sri Lanka. The site began with a small Dutch-period place of worship, and the present building replaced an older church that was in danger of collapsing. The loft also holds a pipe organ given in 1934.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, inside St. Lucia's Cathedral, up in the choir loft. Face down the nave toward the sanctuary and the Archbishop's throne.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific spot where a visitor should stand with the cathedral behind them, so I have not listed any selfie spot. The pages describe the facade and dome as photo subjects (airial.travel, sources: https://airial.travel/attractions/sri-lanka/colombo/st-lucias-cathedral-d6WX_vX8) and mention the front area and the statue of Mary there (tripadvisor.com, https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g293962-d4091814-Reviews-St_Lucia_s_Cathedral-Colombo_Western_Province.html), but none names a standing position for a selfie. For a passer-by shot, yamu.lk (https://yamu.lk/place/st-lucias-cathedral/review-30099) mentions a huge parking lot out front and the dome seen from a distance when heading down Bonjean Road, but it does not say either is a photo spot, so I left ask_someone_spot as null. A Wikimedia Commons photo has a camera location at 6.948389, 79.864944, but it is a coordinate with no named place, so I did not use it. Address-level context found: St Benedict's Street, Kotahena (mapcarta.com) and St Lucia's Street (Flickr). No page states selfie stick or tripod rules, and none gives a selfie safety point. Sources have mixed completion dates for the cathedral (1881, 1887–1902, 1902), which I did not need for this task. Visitor advice found on gpsmycity.com (https://www.gpsmycity.com/attractions/st-lucias-cathedral-43350.html) is to dress modestly and stay quiet and respectful, which is conduct rather than safety, so I left the safety field blank. The cathedral was also reported to be undergoing restoration (wanderlog.com), which could affect the facade for photos.

card.hook: Picture a long white row of columns, all lined up like very polite soldiers, with a big open lawn in front and sea air behind you. That's the Old Parliament Building, and it's made for a tidy photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Galle Face Green, at the northern end of the green, facing the building. From there you look north across the open lawn at the whole front and its colonnade.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole facade and colonnade with the lawn in front. Try 2x or more to pick out the columns, the coat of arms or the statues. Use 0.5x only if you walk much closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the horizontal lines so the building sits level, with a band of lawn at the bottom and some sky at the top.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise or sunset, when warm light falls on the columns. The white walls look lovely then.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the northern end of Galle Face Green, with the building behind you as you look out toward the sea. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and let the colonnade sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the Galle Face Green promenade (seafront side), then pose with the building behind you so they can frame the whole colonnade from the green.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working government building (the Presidential Secretariat), so shoot the exterior from outside the fence. Photography rules near it seem to vary, so check on site. Keep security posts out of your pictures, take photos discreetly, stay clear of the gates and fence, and leave your drone at home.
card.challenge: Can you get every column dead level against the gridlines, with a neat strip of lawn below and sky above?
card.good_to_know: The building opened on 29 January 1930 for the Legislative Council of Ceylon and was designed by Austin Woodeson of the Public Works Department. Parliament sat here for 53 years, until the move to Sri Jayawardenepura in 1983. For a second view, walk to the pavement on Sir Baron Jayatilleke Mawatha to photograph the front garden's bronze statues, including D. S. Senanayake, the first Prime Minister of Ceylon.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Galle Face Green, at the northern end of the green, facing the building. From there you look north across the open lawn at the whole front and its colonnade.

card.hook: The best thing about Colombo Town Hall is the grass in front of it. All that open lawn lets you step back far enough to fit the whole long white front and the dome in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Viharamahadevi Park, around the central fountain area. The Town Hall is about 277 m to the east, so face east and look across the lawns at the white colonnaded front.
card.zoom: Start at 1x from the fountain area. It fits the building and dome with room to spare. If you walk closer and it no longer fits, try 0.5x, or use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the dome or the row of columns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the porch and dome on the middle line, and tap the white front, then slide it a little darker so the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning, before about 9 am, gives soft light on the building, and late afternoon is also good. Take extra care in the park after dark.
card.selfie_here: Head to the park's central fountain area, which a travel guide says gives a clear, unobstructed view of the facade. Use the front camera with the Town Hall over your shoulder, and try 0.5x if you want the columns and dome to fit behind you. The lawn in front of the building, facing the Sir Henry Steele Olcott statue, is another spot where visitors take photos.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the park side opposite the Town Hall front, where they can fit the whole building and dome in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photographing the outside is generally allowed from the park and public pavements. The Town Hall is a working building and the inside is usually closed, so stick to exterior shots.
card.challenge: Count the six tall columns on the main porch in your photo, and see if you can keep every one of them standing straight.
card.good_to_know: S. J. Edwards designed the Town Hall, and his plan won an international competition in 1922. It takes its cue from the Capitol in Washington, D.C. The foundation stone was laid on 24 May 1924, and it opened on 9 August 1928. It's still home to the Colombo Municipal Council and the mayor's office.

card.hook: The Dutch heard jackals in the marshy ground here and decided they were wolves, so this church ended up named 'Wolf's Dale'. Today it's a calm white building on a rise in Pettah, and the wolves are long gone.
card.stand_here: Stand at Wolvendaal Church, right at the church boundary by the old gates, where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the gates so the Dutch East India Company (VOC) emblem is in front of you and the white church is behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the gate, the emblem and the church behind it. Then try 2x or more (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of just the emblem.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the emblem on one third of the frame, then tap the emblem and slide the brightness down a touch so the white walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the white walls. Sundays have services, so expect worshippers and keep your phone use discreet.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the street-side pavement in front of the original VOC gates with the church facade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt up slightly so the gates and the building both fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the opposite pavement of Wolfendhal Street, far enough back to fit the whole facade, dome and roofline, while you stand in front of the gates.
card.rules_and_safety: Photographing the exterior is generally allowed. Ask permission before taking photos inside, especially during services, and note that a small fee may be charged for photography inside. The church may be closed, so be ready to stay with the exterior views.
card.challenge: Hunt down the VOC emblem on the gate and get it sitting neatly on a third of your frame, with the church looking soft and snowy behind it.
card.good_to_know: Wolvendaal is one of the most important Dutch colonial-era buildings in Sri Lanka and one of the oldest Protestant churches still in use. Its foundations were laid in 1749 and it was dedicated for worship on 6 March 1757. It's built in a plain Doric style on a Greek-cross plan, with walls nearly 1.5 m thick and a tall central roof that looks like a dome.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Wolvendaal Church, right at the church boundary by the old gates, where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the gates so the Dutch East India Company (VOC) emblem is in front of you and the white church is behind it.
